title: Phân công chăm sóc không lương · Problems / Solutions
prompt: Some societies are considering giving public pension credits for years spent providing unpaid care. What problems could this create, and what measures could be taken to address them?
instructions: Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.

outline.purpose: Đề yêu cầu vấn đề do chính sách tạo ra và biện pháp khắc phục; phải nối từng giải pháp với nguyên nhân gây hại, thay vì quay sang chứng minh lợi ích hoặc chỉ kêu gọi quản lý tốt. Với “Phân công chăm sóc không lương”, cần xử lý cụ thể: Không nghĩ ghi nhận chăm sóc tự làm phân công bình đẳng. Nếu chủ yếu phụ nữ nghỉ việc, tín chỉ có thể giảm thiệt hại nhưng vẫn củng cố kỳ vọng giới.
outline.content: Unpaid carers sustain essential family support while pension systems often reward only time spent in paid employment. The main problem is that credits alone may entrench expectations that one gender should provide most unpaid care; eligibility should be gender-neutral and accompanied by accessible formal care services.

vocabulary.meaning: phần quyền lợi hưu trí được ghi nhận cho thời gian đủ điều kiện
vocabulary.example: A mother may receive pension credits yet remain unable to return to work because local care services are unavailable, so the reform reduces one financial penalty without removing the pressure behind her career interruption.
vocabulary.note: Chăm người thân tạo giá trị xã hội nhưng nghỉ việc làm giảm năm đóng hưu. Tín chỉ chăm sóc nối hoạt động không lương với bảo vệ thu nhập tuổi già, thay vì coi khoảng đó không đóng góp. Cụm này gọi đúng cơ chế riêng của chính sách; cần giữ nghĩa trong ví dụ, không dùng thay cho việc giải thích quan hệ nhân quả.

vocabulary.example: A carer could retain pension entitlement while supporting a disabled family member.
vocabulary.note: Quyền được hưởng trong hệ hưu trí, khác lương hiện tại; credits bảo vệ tương lai tài chính nhưng không tự giải quyết tổn thất nghề nghiệp.

paragraphs: Unpaid carers sustain essential family support while pension systems often reward only time spent in paid employment. The main problem is that credits alone may entrench expectations that one gender should provide most unpaid care; eligibility should be gender-neutral and accompanied by accessible formal care services.

Credits alone may entrench expectations that one gender should provide most unpaid care. If affordable care alternatives remain unavailable, credits can make prolonged withdrawal from paid work appear the normal solution for one gender. A mother may receive pension credits yet remain unable to return to work because local care services are unavailable, so the reform reduces one financial penalty without removing the pressure behind her career interruption. The pension loss is reduced, but unequal career opportunities and household expectations may persist, limiting the reform's effect on the wider distribution of caring.

Eligibility should be gender-neutral and accompanied by accessible formal care services. Authorities should allow eligible carers of any gender to claim credits and provide usable formal services, evaluating both retirement protection and access to employment rather than treating longer periods outside paid work as evidence of success. Tracking whether carers of different genders can resume employment would show whether services preserve choice, because higher credit uptake alone may simply record that more people have no realistic alternative to leaving paid work for family care. Gender-neutral rules and formal services should accompany credits, ensuring that compensation for caring does not quietly become a policy expectation that women leave paid work. The policy should protect retirement income while preserving a genuine choice between paid work and caring, rather than make withdrawal from employment the expected role of one gender.

Care credits are justified as protection against retirement poverty arising from necessary unpaid work, with success depending on whether carers retain real choices; compensating a contribution should not make a particular gender permanently responsible for supplying it.
